newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybeans up on dry weather, gasoline soars.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybeans up on dry weather, gasoline soars.

text.p: Corn and soybean prices rose sharply on Tuesday in reaction to forecasts for dry weather in the Midwest which could add stress to crops.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November closed 17-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $6.36-1/2 and corn for December delivery rose 8-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $2.60-1/4.

Weather forecasts called for a cool week followed by warmer temperatures this weekend, with no significant chance of rain seen for Illinois until August 6. That would mean a heightened threat to soybeans as pods begin forming on plants.
"New crop is a function of weather," Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc, said. "We're going to go up every day until it rains, then we're going limit down."
In weekly state crop progress ratings issued late on Monday, the U.S. Agriculture Department showed no improvement in soybean ratings despite last week's rains.

Soybeans for August delivery closed at $7.67, up only 9-1/4 cents a bushel, after cash merchandisers and processors in the Midwest reporting a large pickup in farmer sales of remaining soybean stocks.

"The old crop and the new crop started to decouple a little bit because the cash market is crashing on heavy farm movement," Biedermann said. "The demand for the old crop beans has gone downhill. Farmers seem to be letting go."
Corn traders also cited a jump in buying by professional fund speculators who watch trends on price charts.
"I think the market had broken too far basically on perfect weather conditions, it had broken to a weather discount," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst for E.D. and F. Man International.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, cotton prices also rose as concern about dryness overcame recent good crop progress.
Cotton for December delivery rose 0.39 cent a pound to close at 75.41 cents.
"The crop is catching up like a gangbuster but a lot of dryland cotton has to get rain," said O.A. Cleveland, a cotton marketing specialist with Mississippi State University.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline prices ended sharply higher on expectations that weekly U.S. oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday night would show strong demand caused a decline in gasoline stocks.
"We could see a two to three million barrel decline and I think that was built into the market," said Mike De Luca, trader with Prudential Securities.

Gasoline for August delivery closed 1.63 cents a gallon higher at 66.47 cents. Crude and heating oil followed gasoline higher, with September crude closing up four cents at $19.85 a barrel and September heating oil up 0.17 cent at 54.31 cents.

Gasoline traders also cited concern about possible tighter prompt supplies on expectations that production at a 140,000 barrel a day catalytic cracker at Tosco Corp's Bayway refinery would be curtailed due to maintenance at the facility.
The cat cracker at Tosco's Linden, New Jersey, Bayway refinery is the largest in the world and has earned the refinery the moniker of "The Gasoline Machine."

Palladium prices rose to new life-of-contract highs on jitters about future supply from Russia, the leading world supplier. Palladium for September delivery at the NYMEX rose $1.30 an ounce to close at $194.90.

Prices followed the lead of the gains at the Tokyo Commodity Exchange overnight tied to about future Russian supplies after news that Russia's precious metal export agency, Almaz, may close its Tokyo office.
Russia recently resumed paltinum and palladium deliveries after halting them suddenly last December.
